teach.title: What it does
teach.say: A direct question stands on its own: *Quid facit?* — what is he doing? Fold it into a bigger sentence and you get **an indirect question (a question folded into a sentence: nesciō quid faciat = I don't know what he is doing)**. Two things happen and no more: the question mark goes, and the verb moves into the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). English folds questions the same way — 'Where is he?' becomes 'I don't know where he is'.

check.ask: What kind of clause is quid puerī faciant?

teach.title: The question word keeps its place
teach.say: Whatever asked the question stays at the head of the folded clause: *quis* who, *quid* what, *quem* whom, *cūr* why, *ubi* where, *quandō* when, *unde* from where, *quot* how many. Nothing is added and nothing is dropped. *quis* and *quid* are the nominative (the subject form) of that little word: *quis* covers 'who' for a man and for a woman alike, *quid* is the neuter 'what', and *quem* is the accusative (the object form).

check.ask: quot opens this clause. Is it still a folded question?

teach.title: The verb turns subjunctive
teach.say: The only change to the verb is its mood. *Rogat quid puerī faciunt* is not Latin; *rogat quid puerī faciant* is. Take the indicative you would have used and move it into the present subjunctive: *venit* becomes *veniat*, *portat* becomes *portet*, *redit* becomes *redeat*.

check.ask: Give veniō the mood a folded question needs.

teach.title: Yes-or-no questions
teach.say: A question with no question word is opened by *num*, 'whether': *rogat num Dāvus vīnum bibat*. When two possibilities are offered, Latin writes *utrum … an*, 'whether … or': *nesciō utrum dormiat an vigilet*. The verbs are subjunctive exactly as before.

check.ask: utrum … an opens this one. What kind of clause is it?

teach.title: Not a relative clause
teach.say: *quis* and *quid* ask a question; *quī, quem, quae* point back to a noun already named. The mood settles which you are looking at: a folded question has a subjunctive verb, a relative clause keeps the indicative. In *nesciō quis sit puer quem vidēs*, *quis sit* is the question and *quem vidēs* merely describes the boy.

check.ask: Two q-words here. What is the clause ubi sīs doing?

teach.title: Present now, imperfect for the past
teach.say: The tense follows the main verb. A present verb of asking or knowing takes the present subjunctive: *nesciō cūr lacrimet*. A past one takes the imperfect subjunctive (the '-rem, -ret' subjunctive): *nesciēbam cūr lacrimāret*, *rogāvit ubi esset*.

check.ask: rogāvit is past. Which tense of the subjunctive does sum need?

core.text: A question can be asked straight (*Quid facit?* what is he doing?) or tucked inside another sentence — **an indirect question (a question folded into a sentence: nescio quid faciat = I don't know what he is doing)**. After a verb of asking, knowing or wondering (*rogat*, *scit*, *mīrātur*), the question word stays (*quis, quid, cūr, ubi, quōmodo, num*) but the verb goes into the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). Latin name: *interrogātiō oblīqua*.
English: *Where is he?* becomes *I don't know where he is*: only the word order changes. Latin changes the verb form instead.
Asking / knowing verb + question word + subjunctive: present after a present main verb, imperfect after a past one. 'Whether' is num or utrum … an.

invented.en: I did not know why the girl was crying.

core.text: *quis / quid* asks; *quī / quae / quod* (who, which) points back to a noun and keeps the indicative (the plain statement form): *nesciō quid dīcat* (I don't know what he is saying — question) but *audiō id quod dīcit* (I hear what he says — a 'who / which' clause on a noun).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: a reported statement uses the accusative + infinitive (the 'that …' clause after says / sees / thinks) — *dīcit eum venīre*, he says that he is coming; a reported question uses a question word + subjunctive — *rogat num veniat*, he asks whether he is coming. 'That' → infinitive; 'whether / who / why' → subjunctive.

The learner's notes: an indirect question is a question that forms a dependent clause inside another sentence; English marks it by word order, Latin by the subjunctive. Their examples: *sciunt ubi sīs* (they know where you are), *quaere ab eō quō eat* (ask him where he is going), *nesciō quid faciam*.

The question word can be *-ne* on the first word (*interrogāvī tuane esset pecūnia* — I asked whether the money was yours, Week 7), or *num* / *an* for 'whether'. For a question about something already over, the perfect subjunctive follows a present verb (*nesciō quis advēnerit*, Week 10) and the pluperfect a past one (*nesciēbam quis advēnisset*, Week 12). A deliberative question keeps its subjunctive when folded in: *nesciēbat quid faceret* — he did not know what to do. Ørberg's chapter 29 builds the pattern from *Quid faciam?* to *nesciō quid faciam*; chapter 32 adds *dubitat num … laudāverit*.
